opus-5.5.text:
I think the key insight is that interaction gives the model a kind of grounding that passive data alone can't provide. When you watch a video of someone opening a drawer or folding a shirt, there's an enormous amount of information there about how the world works, what objects are, how things move, what people are trying to accomplish. But it's very hard to extract the part that's actually useful for acting if you've never acted yourself. You don't know which details matter. You don't know what the person was feeling through their fingertips, or what would have happened if they'd done something slightly different.

Once a model has some experience actually interacting with the world, even a modest amount, it develops a kind of frame of reference. It understands what it means to grasp something, to apply force, to recover from a mistake. And then when it looks at video, it can interpret that video through the lens of its own embodiment. It's a bit like how a person who has played a little tennis gets much more out of watching a professional match than someone who has never picked up a racket. The novice sees people hitting a ball back and forth; the person with some experience sees footwork, grip, timing, and can actually take something away and try it.

So I see it less as robotic data versus video data, and more as robotic data being the thing that unlocks the value of everything else. The robot experience tells the model what the questions are, and then the vast amount of video and other external data can help answer them. Without the interaction, video is mostly useful for learning representations or predicting what happens next in a fairly generic way. With interaction, the model can start asking, "how would I do that?" and that's where you get real transfer.

There's also a nice feedback loop. As the model gets better from absorbing external data, it can attempt more ambitious things in the real world, which generates more informative experience, which in turn makes it better at leveraging the next batch of passive data. I think that loop, rather than any single data source, is what's going to let these embodied foundation models scale the way language models have.

r001.rationale: The response says interaction helps the model identify useful details and tells it what questions to ask of video. It mentions that video shows what people are trying to accomplish, but does not clearly connect understanding their goals to identifying what to learn from external data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions for the field right now, because the data situation in robotics is so different from the data situation in language or vision. If you're training a language model, the internet basically hands you the data. In robotics, there's no internet of robot experience sitting out there. So the natural thing people say is, well, there's all this video of people doing things, let's just learn from that.

And I think that's right, but with a big caveat. Video tells you what the world looks like and how it tends to evolve, but it doesn't tell you what it feels like to be an agent acting in that world. There's no action labels, there's no sense of what it's like to apply a force and have something unexpectedly happen. So you have this huge source of knowledge that's sort of missing the one ingredient robots care about most, which is the causal connection between what I do and what happens next.

The way I think about it is that robotic interaction is the thing that grounds all that other data. If a robot has even a modest amount of its own experience, where it took an action and saw a consequence, that becomes a kind of Rosetta stone. It lets the model figure out how to map the patterns it saw in human video onto its own body and its own actuators. You can think of it as the video providing the priors, the broad understanding of objects and physics and how tasks are typically structured, and the interaction data providing the calibration, the thing that says, here's how those abstract patterns cash out when it's actually me doing it.

And there's a second piece that I think gets underappreciated, which is that interaction lets the model correct its mistakes. Passive data has this fundamental problem that you only ever see the distribution of what people chose to do. You never see what happens when you make a slightly wrong move and have to recover. A policy trained purely on demonstrations tends to be brittle for exactly that reason. Once the robot is out there acting, it gets to visit the states that no human bothered to record, and it gets to learn from them. So reinforcement learning, or really any kind of autonomous improvement, becomes the mechanism that takes a model with good priors from video and turns it into something robust.

So I'd frame it as a loop rather than a one-way pipeline. External data bootstraps the robot so that it can act competently enough to collect useful experience. That experience then teaches the model how to interpret and exploit the external data better. And as you scale, the robot's own experience starts to become a serious data source in its own right. I think the systems that end up working are the ones that treat these as complementary rather than asking which one is the real answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes video as providing broad priors and interaction as grounding or calibration, but does not state that knowing the goal helps the model identify what to learn from external data.

astra-6.text:
I think robotic interaction can provide a grounding signal for all of that other data. A video shows you what happened, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what you could do to make it happen. You see somebody pick up a cup, but you don’t observe the forces, and you might not even be able to tell exactly how their fingers are contacting it. Those distinctions matter a lot when you actually have to perform the action.

When a robot interacts with the world, it gets data that connects its actions to their consequences. The hope is that this gives it a way to interpret the much larger amount of observational data available in videos. Its own experience might teach it what grasping means in terms of control, while video exposes it to a much wider variety of objects, situations, and ways of accomplishing tasks.

There’s an interesting question about how much interaction you need to make that connection. You wouldn’t want the robot to have to independently rediscover everything it has seen in a video. You’d like a relatively limited amount of experience to teach it how to extract useful knowledge from observations, and then use that knowledge in new situations.

So I think the two sources of data are complementary. Interaction provides a way to test whether the model’s understanding actually supports action. Video provides breadth that would be very expensive to obtain entirely through robots. The challenge is getting that transfer to work reliably.

r001.rationale: The response says interaction can help a model extract useful knowledge from observations, but it does not state that knowing what it is trying to accomplish helps the model identify what to learn from external data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that robotic interaction gives you a way to ground what you see in what you can actually do. A video contains a tremendous amount of information about the world, but it doesn’t generally tell you what commands were sent to the robot, what forces were applied, or what would have happened if the actor had done something different.

If you have some experience interacting with the world yourself, you can start to connect those observations to actions. You’ve tried picking things up, you’ve seen what happens when you push something, and now when you watch a video, you have some basis for interpreting it in terms of your own capabilities. The video doesn’t need to provide every detail of the control problem. It might tell you what a useful sequence of events looks like, while your interaction data tells you how to produce those events.

So I would view these sources of data as complementary. We probably don’t want to learn everything from robot interaction, because that would be enormously expensive. But we also shouldn’t assume that learning from video alone will automatically give us a system that can act. The interesting question is how much grounded experience you need before the model can start getting substantially more value out of all that external data. If that experience lets it interpret videos in terms of actions and consequences, then a relatively limited amount of robot data could potentially unlock a much larger amount of observational data.

r001.rationale: The response says videos can show useful event sequences and interaction data can connect observations to actions, but it does not state that knowing the intended accomplishment helps the model identify what to learn from external data.
